synthesis: The source transports RH into several distinct control problems: square-root-scale prime-counting error, Möbius cancellation, Hilbert-space approximation, and series, determinant, or divisor-sum criteria. Read together, the stated lack of a direct route through prime counting and the failure of the stronger Mertens bound show that logical equivalence does not rank these representations by proof fertility.
source_support: The prime-counting unit states an RH-equivalent error bound but says no other direct approach to pi(x) is apparent. The Möbius unit derives the RH-equivalent M(x) bound through 1/zeta and partial summation, then records that the stronger pointwise Mertens conjecture was disproved. The Nyman-Beurling unit gives density and finite Dirichlet-polynomial distance formulations, while the final equivalence unit lists series-decay, determinant, and divisor-inequality criteria.
nonparaphrase_operation: Compares what multiple truth-preserving translations expose as controllable intermediate objects, then uses one explicit methodological impasse and one failed strengthening to separate representational choice from logical equivalence.
limits: The source proves no criterion easier or more fertile and supplies no selection rule. The disproved claim is the pointwise Mertens inequality; O(sqrt(x)) is only reported as likely false. Several exponents, norms, infima, constants, and inequalities are OCR-sensitive, so only the prose-supported mechanisms and representational comparison are secure.
quality_reason: Accepted because four distinct units jointly establish exact reformulations and, unlike a generic representation theme, two units supply concrete evidence that equivalence can leave the proof burden unchanged or tempt an invalid strengthening.

synthesis: The RMT correspondence is progressively calibrated across observables: GUE pair correlation models local zero spacings, high-zero computation tests that prediction, characteristic polynomials extend the model from locations to zeta-value moments, and family symmetry selects orthogonal, symplectic, or unitary Haar ensembles whose statistics predict moments, value distributions, and central vanishing. This breadth makes the model quantitatively testable without turning it into a proof of RH.
source_support: Montgomery's normalized pair statistic is identified with the GUE eigenvalue correlation and generalized conjecturally to all zero statistics; Odlyzko's computations report large finite agreement. Keating and Snaith compute Haar-unitary characteristic-polynomial moments and match the residual zeta moment constants. Katz and Sarnak connect L-function families and finite-field monodromy to symmetry types, and the family-RMT unit says the correct Haar measure changes predictions and yields precise conjectures including central double-zero frequencies.
nonparaphrase_operation: Lifts one statistical analogy from eigenvalue spacings to characteristic-polynomial values, then conditions the comparison ensemble on family symmetry so that different observables provide mutually constraining, falsifiable tests.
limits: The pair-correlation derivation and the zeta/family predictions remain conjectural, finite computations do not establish an infinite statement, and the source explicitly identifies no Hilbert-Polya operator or route to an RH proof. Number-field monodromy is unknown; several validations depend on unavailable figures and formula-sensitive normalizations.
quality_reason: Accepted because the units support a concrete sequence of model extensions and calibration checks, not merely repeated mentions of RMT, while the candidate retains the source's explicit boundary between predictive agreement and spectral realization or proof.

synthesis: A possible Landau-Siegel zero is the common bottleneck behind several otherwise different methods. Excluding it would remove the ineffectivity in class-number control, while separate source-stated implications reduce that exclusion to crossing a fixed margin below the Brun-Titchmarsh constant 2, below one-half average zeta-zero spacing with the required recurring quantifier, or above one-half nonvanishing in a specified modular family. Across these methods, reaching the boundary is substantial but not enough.
source_support: The class-number units reduce effective lower bounds to control of near-one real zeros and explain how the possible exceptional member makes Siegel's constant ineffective even while repelling other zeros. The sieve unit says any fixed lowering of 2 eliminates the exceptional zero. The gap unit requires, for every sufficiently large T, a consecutive pair in [T,2T] below (1/2-delta) average spacing and reports methods stopping at one-half. The modular-family unit says a proportion above 1/2+delta would eliminate the zero but reports exactly 50 percent.
nonparaphrase_operation: Aligns three conditional threshold bridges and an effectiveness consequence through their shared exceptional-zero variable, revealing a recurring positive-margin obstruction while preserving the different antecedents and quantifiers.
limits: The source does not make the sieve, gap, and nonvanishing statements equivalent to one another, show that an improvement in one transfers to another, or identify which threshold is tractable. The numerical results are source-dated, and damaged displays prevent exact reuse of some ranges, exponents, and constants without scan verification.
quality_reason: Accepted because each threshold unit explicitly points to elimination of the same Landau-Siegel obstruction and the class-number units explicitly connect that obstruction to ineffectivity; their conjunction supports a concrete shared-bottleneck synthesis rather than an unsupported causal story.

synthesis: The source gives two linked ways to turn central multiplicity and family structure into leverage. Goldfeld's idea, realized with Gross-Zagier triple-zero examples, converts extra central vanishing into an effective class-number bound. Iwaniec instead engineers a family with forced double vanishing, combines its coefficients to approximate the Möbius function, and moves the remaining burden to family moments and uniform cancellation estimates. The finite-field family analogy and Conrey's conclusion motivate arithmetic geometry as a source of such structure, but do not complete the number-field program.
source_support: The structural-template unit identifies Euler products and functional equations across L-functions. The family-symmetry unit reports that finite-field monodromy and families enter proofs of individual finite-field RH while their number-field analogue is unknown. The Goldfeld unit states that multiple, unlike simple, central vanishing produces a diverging effective class-number lower bound and records the triple-zero partial victory. The Iwaniec unit explicitly uses forced double zeros and linear combinations of family coefficients to approximate mu, conditional on moment and incomplete exponential-sum estimates. The conclusion proposes families, modularity, moments, arithmetic-geometric exponential sums, and computation as prospective ingredients.
nonparaphrase_operation: Repurposes multiplicity from an exotic obstruction into an amplifier, then enlarges an individual L-function to a varying family so geometric constraints become coefficient combinations and averageable analytic quantities.
limits: Goldfeld's effective class-number result is a completed partial victory and must not be conflated with Iwaniec's unproved reduction toward eliminating the exceptional zero or with Conrey's strategic extension toward RH. The needed moment and uniform incomplete-sum estimates are not proved, the number-field monodromy role is unknown, and display-heavy formulas require scan checking.
quality_reason: Accepted because the parents jointly provide the full mechanism—multiplicity changes the strength of a bound, forced family structure supplies coefficients for Möbius approximation, and averaging exposes moment and cancellation targets—while clearly separating established results from conjectural strategy.
